column2: ai.music(request, [{gen=, seed=1, key=, minor=, bpm=, bars=, inst=, context=}])
column4: **music** for a sound bank (`src/ai/music.c`): rhythms, backing tracks (drums, bass and chords), bass lines, arpeggios, melodies and classic sound effects, 87 recipes. The words choose the recipe (`"rock beat"`, `"lofi backing"`, `"sad melody"`, `"coin sound"`), the key (`"in A minor"`, `"la minore"`), the tempo (`"120 bpm"`, `"fast"`), the length (`"8 bars"`) and the instrument (`"with the piano"`, `"8 bit"`); another `seed` is a variant. The melodies are written by a small network trained on traditional tunes and tunes written for bm. `context = {notes = {…}, bars = {…}}`: the notes already there (MIDI) and the bar of each: melodies, arpeggios and bass lines take their key and chords. Returns `{gen, name, kind, bpm, swing, key, minor, meter, bars, echo, room, seed, chords = {"Am", …}, instruments = {"kick", …}, patterns = { {len, tracks = {[0..7] = {step, …}}} }, sfx = {ms, loop = {a, b}, steps = {step, …}}}`; a step is `note \| instrument << 8 \| vol << 16 \| fx << 24` (instrument: 0-based index into `instruments`). On the RGB30 too, where the words choose the recipe without the network. `ai.music_recipes()` lists them

The kernel checks them first; `model()`, `animate()`, `zone()` and `zboxes()` use the new ones at once and `cart_save` writes them. So bm Studio, bm Animator and bm Pixel change models, skeletons, zones and hitboxes (with `spack` / `sunpack`)

The code runs **apart** (a Lua state of its own, `src/bm/meshcap.c`): the file's body, then `_init`, `_update` and `_draw` once, with an instruction limit; bm's other functions do nothing (no files, screen or sound). The name is that of the variable holding the mesh (`M.ship` → `"ship"`; in an array `chef[2].body` → `"chef2_body"`). For bm Mesh

the game tried is a session of the **debugger** (R13, bm Code: F8 and F5): it stops at the lines `breaks` of its `main.lua`, at `breakpoint()` and, with `stop`, at its first line. Stopped, the debugger covers the screen: the code round the line, the function's variables (the locals, then the upvalues in light blue), the stack; F10 or A the next line (over the calls), F8 or X into the call, Shift+F8 or Y out of the function, F5 or Start goes on, Esc or Select stops the game (which ends with `main.lua:N: stopped in the debugger`: the tool comes back on the line); the arrows scroll the variables and choose the function of the stack. Every game tried from a tool with `cart_run` is a session: without lines it costs nothing until it reaches `breakpoint()`

writes a `.bm` with the code given and the current sprite sheet, tile flags, zones with their boxes, map with its layers, cover, sound bank, models and skeletons (the other sections of the file opened stay as they were; a **SHEET8** sheet nothing was drawn on since `cart_load` goes back as the file had it, byte for byte, else the sheet is written whole as SHEET); an 8.3 name, e.g. `"/bme/game.bme"`. `true` (and the file written when it is not `path`: a game's editable copy, see above), or `false` and a message

the width and height of the project's sprite sheet; with `w` and `h` (multiples of 8, from 8 to 4096) it gets that size: the pixels that fit stay where they are, the new ones are transparent (bm Pixel); the flags stay with their tile

leaves and opens another tool of the console on the same file: `"studio"`, `"animator"`, `"mesh"`, `"pixel"`, `"code"`, `"sdk"`, `"sound"` (bm Studio → *Open in bm Animator*, and back); the tool finds it in `cart_arg()` as from the menu, with `from` = the name of the tool that opened it (`"sdk"`: the suite's menus offer *Back to bm SDK*)

column2: cart_write(path, {[lua, title, author, res, from, sections]})
column4: changes **only** the code (and the data fields) of a `.bm`: sprite sheet, map, cover, sound bank and the sections the kernel does not know stay as they were; a file with a long name keeps it. Without `lua` the code stays as it is. A file that is not there becomes a cartridge with only the code (an 8.3 name). `from`: the other sections come from another file ("save as"); `from = false`: a new cartridge, whatever the file holds (bm Studio's new project). `sections`: `{[8] = MESH bytes, [9] = ANIM bytes, [11] = SPRITES bytes}` (`false` takes them away), checked first (`false, "broken MESH section"`): so bm Mesh writes the models and bm Pixel's Stack page writes the zones. `sheet = true`: the project's sprite sheet (`cart_load`, `sset`, `cart_sheet`) takes the place of the file's, as **SHEET8** when it has at most 256 colours (otherwise SHEET), with the colours of `palette` (`{0xRRGGBB, …}`) first in its palette, as they are and in that order (the transparent entry of the palette of before stays in its place); a pixel that still has the RGB565 it had in the file keeps its 24 bits of before (the console keeps 16 bits per pixel): only the pixels drawn again change. So bm Pixel saves the sheet. If `fset` changed some flags meanwhile, those go into the file too. Returns like `cart_save`

`bands, floor, outline_rgb, outline_width`: **cel light** (bm3D 7.4). `bands` 0 or `false` is off (default); 2-8 cuts the sun light of the `draw3d` calls with flag 256 into that many bands. `floor` 0-1 (default 0.35) is the sun term of the darkest band. `outline_rgb` (`0xRRGGBB`, `nil`/`false` none) and `outline_width` (0.005-0.05, default 0.02) are used by the outline flag 512: the colour of the outline and its thickness as a share of the mesh's size (the width of the mesh's sphere), seen from outside the mesh. Every call sets all four. With no argument it returns the values in force. The ambient and sky light stay smooth, the `shine3d` highlight becomes one step (on above 0.5), lamps (`lamp3d`) are not cut. The file has the same bytes as `scripts/bmres.py` makes (header, CRC-32, section table in the order MESH, ANIM, sheet, INFO). The editors use `T.write_bmm` of `src/script/bm3d.lua`
every voice **8-bit** as in the first versions (naive waves, straight envelopes, no room nor echo) while the game runs; returns whether they are (Settings can ask for it too)
the room the voices play in (0–1: a small room to a hall, bright to dull, how much is heard); returns the three. Each voice sends to it what its `reverb` says (a little by default: 0.16)
the colour integer `0xRRGGBB` of three numbers 0-255 (the colours of the API are 24-bit integers: `0xFFFFFF` is white; a small number such as 7 is nearly black)
saves table `t` on the SD card, in slot 1–8 (default 1); `true`, or `false` and the reason (no SD card, card full...)
the table saved last time in that slot (default 1), or `nil`
the slots in use, `{[slot] = bytes}` (e.g. `{[1] = 40, [3] = 212}`), and how many there are (8): for a "load game" page

the cartridge's resolution from the next frame: `true`, or `false` if it is not one of these (16:9): 320×180, 384×216, 480×270, 640×360, 960×540, 1280×720, 1920×1080 (on a 1080p TV all at whole pixels but 1280×720). `SCREEN_W` and `SCREEN_H` change when it is done; the z-buffer, the 3D camera and the light buffers follow, the font and `camera()` stay, `clip()` goes back to the whole screen. If the console cannot give it, the one before stays. `screen()` → the width and height now; `screen(i)` → the i-th of the list (from 1), or `nil`. On the **RGB30** (a square panel) the list is the `.b16`'s two sizes instead, 360×360 (shown twice as big) and 720×720, both at whole pixels. A square cartridge (256×256, 360×360) changes as the others (2026-10-10): on the Pi it then fills the TV, and the GPU can draw its 3D there (in the box in the middle the ARM draws it). The ARM's rasteriser pays for every pixel: on the Pi above 640×360 the GPU is needed

plays sound effect `n` of the bank; without `v` it chooses a free voice, preferring those the music leaves empty. `semitones` transposes it (`sfx(0, nil, 12)`: an octave up), `vol` 0–1. Returns the voice, or `nil` (no bank, a number that is not there)
stops the effect of voice `v`, or all
the effect playing on voice `v` and its step, or `nil`
reads / writes a pixel of the sheet (`nil` = transparent)
the shadows of `draw3d` with flag 8: 0 darken (default), 1 dithered black (without reading the screen)

the **animated GIF of a list of sprite sheet rectangles**, as a string (GIF89a): one frame a rectangle (1 to 64), in the order given, all the same size, drawn one after the other for ever, `delay_cs` hundredths of a second each (1 to 65535, default 10). A pixel the sheet has transparent stays transparent. The colours are the sheet's RGB565 widened to 8 bits and exact when the frames have at most 255 of them; with more, a median cut reduces them to 255. `nil` and the reason when a rectangle is not inside the sheet, the sizes differ, the frames have more than 262144 pixels in all, or there is no memory. The encoder runs only in this call, and its buffers are freed before it returns. bm Pixel's export writes it with `doc_write` or `file_write`

the **PNG file of a rectangle of the sprite sheet**, as a string (colour type 6, RGBA: a pixel the sheet has transparent gets alpha 0, any other alpha 255; the colours are the sheet's RGB565 widened to 8 bits). `nil` and the reason when the rectangle is not inside the sheet, or is larger than 4096, or there is no memory. The pixels are copied to a buffer that is freed before the call returns. bm Pixel's export writes it with `doc_write` or `file_write`

the same for a list of rectangles (1 to 64): they go side by side, left to right, in the order given, in one PNG; all must have the same `h`, and the total width is at most 4096 (`nil` and the reason if not)
the sun's reflections on glossy faces (`spec` 0–2, `exponent` 4–64: higher, smaller) and light on the shapes' rim (`rim` 0–1)

saves the frame being drawn as a PNG in `bm/shots/` when `_draw` ends and returns its name (`"bm/shots/PONG0007.png"`); the name starts with the first letters of the game's title, or of `prefix` (up to 4 letters or digits), then a number. `nil` and a message if the numbers are over. The player has a key for it too (Print Screen; Select held for 3 seconds). [SCREENSHOTS.md](../SCREENSHOTS.md)

opens the keys of `keyhelp()` as F12 held does, but they stay open (for a mouse click on the chip "F12 keys"): a click, F12 or Esc closes them, the arrows turn the pages, and the cartridge gets no other key or button meanwhile. Returns `true` when open. `U.keys()` in `bmui` calls it for the fixed chip of the hint bars
colours (0xRRGGBB) of the sun's light and of the ambient light coming from above and below (faces turned up take the sky, those turned down the ground); `sky3d()` goes back to white
the note slides to `hz` in `ms` (default 100): glissandos, sirens, lasers

plays the event. Returns `false` if the name is unknown, the `gap` is not over, or a tune of a higher `prio` is running. A new tune replaces a tune of the same or a lower `prio`; its first note sounds in the next `snd:update()`
stops the tune
once a frame, first in `_update`: counts the frames and plays the next note of the tune

column2: spr(n, x, y, [w, h, flip_x, flip_y])
column4: draws cell `n` (w×h cells, default 1×1), mirrored too

column2: sprite3d(sx, sy, sw, sh, x, y, z, width, [flags])
column4: a rectangle of the sprite sheet facing the camera, `width` units wide in the world, hidden by the closer things: explosions, smoke, icons over the characters
reads / writes a pixel of the sheet (`nil` = transparent)

column2: sspr(sx, sy, sw, sh, dx, dy, [flip_x, flip_y, zoom])
column4: copies any rectangle of the sheet; with `zoom` (default 1) it draws it bigger (`2`, `3`…) or smaller (`0.5`), pixel by pixel: it covers `sw * zoom` × `sh * zoom` pixels

column2: stack(sx, sy, w, h, n, x, y, [rz, scale, step])
column4: sprite stacking: draws `n` slices of `w`×`h` pixels that lie side by side on the sheet from `(sx, sy)`, left to right. Slice 1 is the bottom and is drawn first. `(x, y)` is the centre of the bottom slice on the ground. Each slice turns by `rz` radians (default 0) around its centre, is `scale` times bigger (default 1) and sits `step * scale` pixels above the slice below (default `step` 1). Colour 0 is transparent. It reads the sheet each call and keeps no memory. At `rz` 0 and `scale` 1 it equals `n` calls of `sspr`. A slice that is not wholly inside the sheet is skipped. `scale` of 0 or less, or above 64, draws nothing. `rz`, `scale` or `step` that is NaN or infinite draws nothing

column2: stackv(sx, sy, w, h, n, x, y, [rz, scale, step])
column4: as `stack`, but the `n` slices lie one under the other on the sheet from `(sx, sy)`, top to bottom: the top one is slice 1, the bottom of the stack. The same drawing, the same limits (a slice that is not wholly inside the sheet is skipped), the same cost

0 KiB used by Lua, 1 ms of the last frame (`_update` + `_draw`, with the GPU's 3D), 2 fps, 3 frame number, 4 3D triangles, 5 3D pixels (0 with the GPU), 6 ms spent in 3D drawing (since `zclear`; with the GPU the ARM's part), 7 3D vertices transformed, 8 ms since the start of this frame (to measure the phases), 9 `1` if the GPU draws the 3D, 10 Lua instructions of the last frame (`_update` + `_draw`; the count, rounded to the thousand); the **dev kit** (2026-10-04): 11 tokens of the cartridge's code (`code_tokens`), 12 the most KiB of Lua of this run, 13 KiB of the cartridge's data in memory (sprite sheet, map, models and skeletons, sound bank, the 3D z-buffer), 14 the Lua instructions of the busiest frame of this run; 15 how many `_update` ran before this `_draw` (1; more with `frameskip`); 16 ms of GPU job time (bin + render) accounted in the last frame, `0` when the ARM draws the 3D (2026-10-12; with `stat(1)` it tells whether the GPU or the ARM sets the pace); the profiling metrics (bm3D 7.x): 17 ms of audio processing in the last frame (the time of the audio interrupt), 18 ms the ARM waited for the GPU in the last frame (time blocked on GPU job completion). Use 1, 16, 17 and 18 together to see if the CPU/ARM or the GPU is the bottleneck. 18 is `0` when the ARM draws the 3D. On the RGB30 and in QEMU, 16 and 18 are `0` (no V3D jobs there), and 17 is `0` where the console has no audio interrupt to time. **A measurement only**: it differs between consoles, so never use it (nor 1, 2, 6, 8, 10, 16, 17, 18) in game logic, or a lockstep match falls out of step

player `p`'s left stick: `x, y` between −1 and 1 (x to the right, y down), with a dead zone; with the keyboard or a pad without a stick it is the cross (8 directions). With `n = 1` the **right** stick (to aim in shooters; `0, 0` without a stick). Without `p`: the one pushed most
the music goes `x` times faster (1 = as written): speed up when the game gets hard

`on`: `textures3d(false)` makes every `draw3d` behave as with flag 128 (textured faces as flat colours, their average texel), `textures3d(true)` goes back to the textures (default); returns the current state. For a "flat / textured" option in a game (bm3d 7.0)
seconds since the cartridge started (with decimals)

coroutine `co` stops by itself after about `k` thousand Lua instructions in a frame (400 if missing) and `coroutine.resume` returns `true` without values: a long computation goes on in the next frames instead of stopping the cartridge at the instruction limit. `timeslice(nil)` takes it away (nano8 uses it for its cartridges)

the voice's tone for the `note()`s that follow: the name of a **ready-made instrument** (`"epiano"`, `"pluck"`, `"pad"`, `"kick"`… `instruments()` lists them) or a table in plain units (below). `tone(v)` goes back to the square of a fresh voice
a filled triangle; with three colours (one per corner) the colour shades from one corner to the other (Gouraud, dithered)
closes the socket

a socket on the port (0 or nothing: any); `nil` and the reason if there is no network or free socket. The first time a game opens one, the player is asked whether it may use the network (the answer stays in `bm/config.txt`); after a no, `nil` and the reason
the next packet that arrived, or `nil`; up to 48 wait in the queue
sends a string (at most 1024 bytes); `true` if it left (UDP: it can be lost)
a vibrato `semitones` wide (for example 0.3) at `hz` swings a second (default 6); `vibrato(v)` takes it away

opens `bm/clips/<name>` (a file name, no path), or `bm/rec/<file>` for a recording when `name` starts with `"rec/"` (`"rec/r0010001.bmv"`). Returns a clip, or `nil` and a message ("no such clip", "the clip is over 48 MiB", "not a .bmv clip" ...). The clip is freed when it is closed or when the game ends

`false` if a sphere (centre, radius) cannot be seen: behind the camera, beyond an edge of the screen, or (after `pvs3d`) on pieces of the map that the camera's cell does not see. To skip the characters and effects hidden by the walls before drawing them (bm3d 5.5)
the general volume 0–10 (with `level` it changes it). It is the console's: it holds for every game and stays in `bm/config.txt`
the body of a finished request as a string, or `nil` and the reason. It copies the bytes into Lua memory: to decode a picture or write a file, give `id` to `image_load` or `file_write` instead
stops the request and frees its result. Returns `true` if it was there

starts a GET request. `opts` is a table: `max` (a body cap in bytes, lower than the configured cap), `timeout` (milliseconds for one read, 1000 to 60000, default 15000), `resume` (a bare 8.3 name in `bm/web`, see Resume above). Returns the request `id`, or `nil` and the reason (bad address, no network, the player said no, a request already runs, no free slot)

a table: `state`, `status` (the HTTP status), `type` (Content-Type), `length`, `location` (the Location header of the last answer), `url` (the address reached), `size`, `resumed` (the bytes that came from the part file) and `error`. Fields that are not known are left out. Any HTTP status ends in `"done"`, a 404 too: look at `status`. A failed request (no connection, a refused redirect, a body over the cap, a timeout) ends in `"error"`

works the request for about 4 ms. `state` is `"wait"` (the pause per host), `"busy"`, `"done"` or `"error"`. `size` is the body bytes received so far. `length` is the Content-Length (`nil` if the server did not give it). `nil` and a reason for an `id` that is not there. Call it once a frame
an empty collision world

column2: world_box(w, x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1, [tag])
column4: a solid box; returns its number
the floor's height under `(x, z)`

column2: world_move(w, x, y, z, r, h, dx, dy, dz, [step, on_ground])
column4: `x, y, z, flags`: a body (feet at `x, y, z`, radius `r`, height `h`) moved by `d`, sliding on the walls and climbing steps up to `step` (0.45) if it was on the ground. `flags`: 1 on the ground, 2 a wall (4 along x, 8 along z), 16 a ceiling

column2: world_ray(w, ox, oy, oz, dx, dy, dz, [maxd, ground])
column4: `t, nx, ny, nz, box`: the first point hit along the ray (the face's normal; box 0 = the ground `y = 0`, which counts unless `ground` is `false`), or `nil`

the **hitboxes and hurtboxes** of the frames of a zone (the BOXES section, 2026-10-04): a list of `{x, y, w, h, kind, frame}`, `x` and `y` from the frame's top left corner (they may stick out), `kind` `"hurt"` (where it can be hit), `"hit"` (where it hurts), `"body"` (the room the body takes) or a number of the game (3–255), `frame` 0 for a box of every frame. With `frame` (from 1; past the last it starts again) its boxes and those of every frame; without, all the zone's. `kind` (a name or a number) keeps one kind. `{}` if there are none; a zone that is not there is an error
clears the z-buffer (every frame, before `draw3d`)
`x, y, w, h, frames, fps, slices` of the zone (its first frame, in sheet pixels), or `nil`. `slices` is 0 for a plain zone, 2 to 255 for a stack zone
the names of the zones, in order (`{}` if there are none)

column4: draws a **named zone** of the sheet (below): `frame` from 1 to the number of frames (beyond it starts again), or `nil`: the one its fps give at `time()`, so the animation runs by itself. Returns the frame drawn. A zone that is not there is an error

draws a **stack zone** (a zone with slices, below) as `stack` does (as `stackv` for a `stackv` zone), with `step` 1: the slices of the zone, `(x, y)` the centre of the bottom one. A zone without slices (or one that is not there) is an error
